mainTopic: Accuracy and safeguards in שטרות: true dates and places, not rewriting loan notes, and the new משנה on shared inheritance and two people with the same name
overview: The amud opens at the end of a discussion about a safeguard against a lender collecting the same debt twice. The answer is that the רבנן set up the safeguard, and anyone who skips it has only hurt himself. Next come rules for scribes: a שטר must give a true date and the true place where it was written, so it never looks like a lie. רבא then rules that בית דין will not split one hundred-זוז שטר into two fifties, or merge two fifties into one hundred, because each setup already balances benefits for the מלוה and the לוה. רב אשי adds that בית דין will not shrink a hundred-זוז שטר into a fifty, because of a possible trick with a receipt for a debt that was already paid. A new משנה follows. It covers two brothers, one rich and one poor, who inherit a bathhouse and an olive press. It also covers two men in one city both named יוסף בן שמעון, and how they should write their names so their שטרות are not confused. The גמרא then begins with a story about a שטר brought to רב הונא's בית דין that does not name the lender.

steps.title: But nowadays people do not follow this safeguard
steps.stepSummary: The questioner challenges the safeguard against double collection: in practice, people today do not do it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But nowadays we do not do this!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the safeguard just described. In real life, people today do not follow it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion described a precaution that protects against a debt being collected twice. The challenge points to common practice. If nobody does it, how can it be the required system, and what protects people who skip it?

phrases.english: But nowadays,
we do not do this!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion from before this section about protecting against double collection of a loan.
steps.kashyaTarget: The safeguard the חכמים set up against double collection
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Common practice ignores the safeguard, so it seems either not binding or not workable.

steps.title: The Sages set it up, and whoever skips it only hurts himself
steps.stepSummary: The answer explains that the רבנן set up the safeguard. Whoever follows it is protected, and whoever skips it causes his own loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The רבנן made an enactment. Whoever follows it, follows it. Whoever does not follow it has caused his own loss.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer is that the safeguard really is a rule of the רבנן. People who ignore it are not protected, and the loss is their own fault.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Common practice does not cancel the rule. The תקנה was made to protect the person paying. If he chooses not to use it, he has given up his own protection, and nobody else is to blame.

keyTerms.meaning: They truly enacted a rule (a תַּקָּנָה)

steps.whatToRemember: A protective תקנה stays valid even if people skip it. Whoever ignores it takes on the risk himself.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a general principle: a protective rule is an option that guards the person who uses it. Neglecting it does not cancel it, and it moves the risk onto the one who neglected it.

phrases.english: He said to him: The Sages instituted an enactment;
one who does it, does it,
one who does not do it,
he is the one who caused a loss to himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the challenge in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing: the rule is a protective option, and ignoring it is the individual's own risk.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since people do not follow the safeguard, maybe it is not a real or binding system.
steps.terutzMaskana: The safeguard is a real תקנה. Anyone who skips it loses its protection by his own choice.

steps.title: Write the real date of the acquisition, or else the day of writing
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב שילא tells scribes of deeds of acquisition to write the actual date of the קנין if they know it. Otherwise they should write the date on which they are writing, so the document does not look false.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר רב שילא said to those scribes who wrote deeds of acquisition: When you write deeds of acquisition, if you know the day on which you made the קנין, write that day. If not, write the day on which you are standing now, so that the document will not look like a lie.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new rule for scribes. A שטר must carry a true date: either the known date of the קנין or the date it is written. A guessed date is not allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sometimes the קנין happened earlier and the deed is written later. Writing the true קנין date is best. If that date is unknown, you may not guess, because a wrong date would make the שטר look false. The day of writing is always a true date, since the קנין had certainly happened by then.

keyTerms.meaning: Deeds of acquisition (documents recording a sale or gift)
You made the קִנְיָן, the formal act of acquiring
You are standing, meaning where or when you are now

steps.confusionAlert: Writing the later date does not change when the קנין happened. It only means the שטר records a date that is surely true.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ רָבָא בַּר רַב שֵׁילָא
phrases.english: Rava bar Rav Sheila said
to those writers of deeds of acquisition:
When you write deeds of acquisition,

phrases.aramaic: אִי יָדְעִיתוּ יוֹמָא דִּקְנֵיתוּ בֵּיהּ – כְּתֻבוּ,
phrases.english: if you know the day on which you acquired, write it;

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי לָא – כְּתֻבוּ יוֹמָא דְּקָיְימִיתוּ בֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: and if not, write the day on which you are standing,
phrases.notes: 'The day you are standing in' just means today, the day the שטר is being written.

phrases.english: so that it should not appear as a falsehood.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רָבָא בַּר רַב שֵׁילָא לְהָנְהוּ כָּתְבֵי שְׁטָרֵי אַקְנְיָאתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new practical rule about scribes and the accuracy of documents.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A deed must carry either the known date of the קנין or the date of writing, never a guessed date, so it does not look false.

steps.title: Write the place where you are actually writing
steps.stepSummary: רב and רב הונא each told his scribe to write in the שטר the town where he is writing it, even if the deal took place in a different town.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to his scribes, and רב הונא likewise said to his scribes: When you are in שילי, write 'in שילי,' even if the matters were given over to you in היני. When you are in היני, write 'in היני,' even if the matters were given over to you in שילי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a matching rule about place. The שטר should name the town where it is written, not the town where the deal was told to the scribe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This matches the date rule in step 3. A שטר records the scribe's own writing, so it must state the true place of writing. Writing a different town would make it look false.

keyTerms.meaning: שילי and הִינֵי, two neighboring towns
The matters were handed over, meaning the deal was given to you to record

steps.whatToRemember: Steps 3 and 4 together teach that a שטר must state a true date and a true place of writing, so it never looks like a lie.

phrases.english: Rav said to his scribes,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב הוּנָא לְסָפְרֵיהּ:
phrases.english: and so too Rav Huna said to his scribes:
When you are situated in Shili, write 'in Shili,'

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל גַּב דִּמְסִירָן לְכוּ מִילֵּי בְּהִינֵי;
phrases.english: even though the matters were given over to you in Hini;
phrases.notes: He means the deal itself happened, or was told to you, in the other town.

phrases.english: when you are situated in Hini, write 'in Hini,'

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל גַּב דִּמְסִירָן לְכוּ מִילֵּי בְּשִׁילֵי.
phrases.english: even though the matters were given over to you in Shili.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב לְסָפְרֵיהּ וְכֵן אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב הוּנָא לְסָפְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a matching rule about place to the date rule of step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שטר records the place where it is actually written, even if the transaction took place elsewhere.

steps.title: We do not split a hundred-זוז note into two fifty-זוז notes
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if someone holding a שטר for one hundred זוז asks בית דין to replace it with two שטרות of fifty each, בית דין does not do it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Someone who holds a שטר of one hundred זוז and says, 'Make it into two שטרות of fifty each for me,' we do not make them for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. רבא rules that בית דין will not split one large שטר into two smaller ones. The next step gives the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender wants two smaller notes, perhaps so a partial payment can be handled by handing back one of them. רבא refuses. This sets up the next part of the גמרא, which will give the reason for the refusal.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not make or prepare

phrases.english: Rava said: This one who holds
a note of one hundred dinars,
and says: Make it for me
into two notes of fifty each,
we do not make them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא הַאי מַאן דִּנְקִיט שְׁטָרָא בַּר מְאָה זוּזֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic about rewriting or dividing a שטר. Step 6 gives the reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית דין does not exchange one שטר of one hundred זוז for two שטרות of fifty זוז each.

steps.title: Why בית דין won't split a 100-זוז note into two 50s
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רבא's ruling from Step 5. Leaving the single big שטר as it is helps both the מלוה and the לוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why not? The רבנן made a rule that helps both the lender and the borrower. It helps the lender because one big note lets him press the borrower to pay. It helps the borrower because if he pays part of it, the note becomes a damaged, partly paid note.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why בית דין refuses to split the hundred-זוז שטר. It answers that keeping one big שטר benefits both sides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מלוה gains because a large debt in one document puts more pressure on the borrower to pay. The לוה gains because once he pays half, the single שטר is marked as partly paid, and a damaged שטר like that is harder for the lender to collect on. So neither side should get to change the setup the רבנן arranged.

keyTerms.meaning: It is good / beneficial for him
He can press (force) him to pay
His document becomes damaged, meaning marked as partly paid

phrases.english: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: He is asking about רבא's ruling just before this: why not split the hundred-זוז note into two fifties?

phrases.english: The Sages made an arrangement
that is good for the lender,
and good for the borrower;

phrases.aramaic: נִיחָא לֵיהּ לְמַלְוֶה – כְּדֵי שֶׁיָּכוֹף לְפוֹרְעוֹ,
phrases.english: good for the lender, so that he can press him to pay,

phrases.aramaic: וְנִיחָא לְלֹוֶה – כִּי הֵיכִי דְּנִיפְגֹּם שְׁטָרֵיהּ.
phrases.english: and good for the borrower, so that his note becomes damaged.
phrases.notes: A "damaged" note is one already marked as partly paid. The lender then has a harder time collecting the rest.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind רבא's ruling in Step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why בית דין refuses to split a hundred-זוז שטר into two fifty-זוז שטרות.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One big שטר helps the lender press for payment, and it helps the borrower because a partial payment leaves the שטר damaged.

steps.title: Two 50-זוז notes are not merged into one 100
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules on the reverse case. Someone holding two fifty-זוז שטרות who asks בית דין to combine them into one hundred-זוז שטר is refused.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא also said: if someone holds two notes of fifty each and says, 'Make them into one note of a hundred for me,' we do not do it for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second ruling that is the mirror image of the first. Combining two small שטרות into one big one is also refused.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 said you cannot split one into two. Now רבא adds that you cannot merge two into one either. The theme is that בית דין does not rewrite the shape of a debt at one side's request.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not make it for him

phrases.english: And Rava said:
This one who is holding
two notes of fifty each,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר: שַׁוִּינְהוּ נִיהֲלִי חַד בַּר מְאָה –
phrases.english: and says: make them for me into one of a hundred,
we do not make it for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא: הַאי מַאן דִּנְקִיט תְּרֵי שְׁטָרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The reverse case of Step 5: merging instead of splitting.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית דין does not combine two fifty-זוז שטרות into one hundred-זוז שטר.

steps.title: Why the two small notes stay separate
steps.stepSummary: The reason is the same idea as before: the current setup helps both sides. This time each side's benefit is reversed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן made a rule that helps both the lender and the borrower. It helps the lender because his note will not become damaged when part is paid. It helps the borrower because the lender cannot press him so hard to pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבא's second ruling. Keeping two separate small שטרות benefits both lender and borrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender gains because if fifty is paid, one whole שטר is simply returned, and the other stays clean and not damaged. The borrower gains because two smaller debts do not give the lender as much pressure as one large one. Each benefit is the exact flip of Step 6.

keyTerms.meaning: That it will not become damaged (partly paid)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two cases. With one big note, the lender gains pressure and the borrower gains a damaged note. With two small notes, the lender gains a clean note and the borrower avoids the pressure.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows one principle behind both rulings: whatever form the debt is in, it already carries balanced benefits, so neither party can ask בית דין to change it.

phrases.english: The Sages made an arrangement
phrases.notes: No "what is the reason" is written here, but this is the reason for רבא's ruling just before.

phrases.english: that is good for the lender,
and good for the borrower;

phrases.aramaic: נִיחָא לֵיהּ לְמַלְוֶה – כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא נִיפְגּוֹם שְׁטָרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: good for the lender, so that his note will not become damaged,

phrases.aramaic: וְנִיחָא לֵיהּ לְלֹוֶה – כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יָכוֹף לְפוֹרְעוֹ.
phrases.english: and good for the borrower, so that he cannot press him to pay.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲבוּד רַבָּנַן מִילְּתָא דְּנִיחָא לֵיהּ לְמַלְוֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning for Step 7, mirroring the reasoning of Step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why בית דין refuses to merge two fifty-זוז שטרות.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Separate notes keep the lender's note from becoming damaged, and they spare the borrower the pressure of one large debt.

steps.title: A 100-זוז note is not rewritten as a 50
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי rules that if someone holds a hundred-זוז שטר and asks בית דין to replace it with one fifty-זוז שטר, בית דין refuses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: if someone holds a note for one hundred זוז and says, 'Make it into one note of fifty for me,' I do not do it for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי adds a new related ruling. A big שטר is not rewritten as a smaller one, even when the holder himself asks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a different case from רבא's. The lender is not splitting or merging. He wants to shrink the note, apparently because half has been paid. The next step gives רב אשי's reason, which is a different concern from רבא's.

keyTerms.meaning: I do not make it for him

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
This one who is holding
a note of one hundred zuz,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר: שַׁוּוֹנְהִי נִיהֲלִי חַד בַּר חַמְשִׁין –
phrases.english: and says: make it for me into one of fifty,
phrases.notes: He is asking for this because the borrower already paid half.

phrases.english: I do not make it for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: הַאי מַאן דִּנְקִיט שְׁטָרָא בַּר מְאָה זוּזֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling by a different אמורא in the same series about rewriting שטרות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית דין does not replace a hundred-זוז שטר with a single fifty-זוז שטר at the holder's request.

steps.title: Why a hundred-זוז שטר is not rewritten as a fifty-זוז שטר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רב אשי's ruling. The לוה may have already paid the whole debt and been given a receipt instead of the old שטר. A new fifty-זוז שטר would let the מלוה say the receipt belongs to some other loan.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? We worry that this happened. The borrower really paid back everything and said, 'Give me my שטר.' The lender said, 'I lost it,' and wrote him a receipt instead. Now the lender will bring out this new fifty-זוז שטר and say, 'That receipt is for a different loan.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב אשי's ruling in Step 9 and answers it right away. It describes a trick the מלוה could pull if בית דין wrote him a new, smaller שטר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A receipt (תברא) for a hundred זוז matches the old hundred-זוז שטר. If בית דין writes a fresh fifty-זוז שטר, the amounts no longer match. Then the מלוה can claim the receipt was for some other debt and collect fifty זוז that were already paid.

keyTerms.meaning: A receipt showing a debt was paid (also called שׁוֹבָר)

steps.whatToRemember: בית דין will not rewrite a שטר in a way that could let a debt that was already paid be collected again.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: He is asking about רב אשי's ruling just before this, that בית דין won't swap a hundred-זוז שטר for a fifty.

phrases.english: We say: this one actually paid him back,
phrases.notes: 'We say' here means 'we worry that this happened.' The borrower paid the whole hundred.

phrases.english: and he said to him: Give me my שטר,
and he said to him: It got lost on me,
and he wrote him a receipt;
and he will bring out this one against him,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the new fifty-זוז שטר that בית דין would have written.

phrases.english: and say to him: That one is for a different loan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for רב אשי's ruling in Step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why won't בית דין replace a hundred-זוז שטר with a fifty-זוז שטר?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The debt may already be fully paid with a receipt given in place of the שטר. A new shorter שטר would let the מלוה claim the receipt was for another loan.

steps.title: A rich brother and a poor brother inherit a bathhouse and an olive press
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה. If the father built the bathhouse and olive press to rent out, the brothers split the profit equally. If he built them for his own use, the rich brother can tell the poor one to bring his own servants and olives and use them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two brothers, one poor and one rich, inherited a bathhouse and an olive press from their father. If the father made them to earn rent, the profit is split down the middle. If he made them for himself, the rich brother can say to the poor brother: 'Get yourself servants and let them bathe in the bathhouse. Get yourself olives and come press them in the olive press.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new topic. Two brothers inherit a bathhouse and an olive press, and the משנה rules on how they share them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everything depends on what the father built them for. If they were built to earn money, that is how they keep running and the profit is shared. If they were built for family use, they stay that way, and the poor brother uses his share by actually using the facilities.

keyTerms.meaning: משנה: the start of a new משנה

steps.confusionAlert: The rich brother is not keeping everything for himself. Both brothers still own the facilities equally. The rich brother is only saying they stay for personal use, so the poor brother uses them himself instead of getting paid.

phrases.english: MISHNA: Two brothers –
one poor and one rich,
and their father left them
a bathhouse and an olive press;
if he made them for profit – the profit is split down the middle.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the father. He built them to charge other people for using them.

phrases.english: If he made them for himself –
the rich one can say to the poor one:
"Take servants for yourself and let them bathe in the bathhouse,
take olives for yourself
and come make oil in the olive press."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה with a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Facilities built for profit: the profit is split equally. Facilities built for personal use: they stay that way, and the poor brother must use them himself.

steps.title: Two people in one city both named יוסף בן שמעון
steps.stepSummary: If two people in the same city are both called יוסף בן שמעון, neither can collect a שטר חוב from the other. An outside person also cannot collect a שטר חוב from either of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two people lived in one city. One was named יוסף בן שמעון, and the other was also named יוסף בן שמעון. They cannot bring a loan document against each other, and no one else can bring a loan document against them.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves to a new case about people with the same name. Because the names match, a שטר חוב against them cannot be collected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שטר identifies people by name, so here it cannot show which יוסף בן שמעון is the lender and which is the borrower. Each man can say the שטר really belongs to the other one, so it cannot be collected.

keyTerms.meaning: To bring out (present a document in בית דין to collect)

phrases.english: Two people who were in one city,
one named "Yosef ben Shimon"
and the other named "Yosef ben Shimon" –
they cannot bring out
a loan document against each other,
phrases.notes: The man being sued can say, 'No, you owed me, you paid, and I gave you back this שטר.'

phrases.english: nor can someone else bring out
a loan document against them.
phrases.notes: Each one can say, 'It's the other יוסף בן שמעון who owes you, not me.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate ruling in the same משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When two people in one city share the same name, no שטר חוב can be collected against either of them, whether by each other or by an outside person.

steps.title: A note saying 'יוסף בן שמעון's שטר is paid' cancels both
steps.stepSummary: If a lender is owed money by both men named יוסף בן שמעון, and a note saying 'יוסף בן שמעון's שטר is paid' is found among his papers, both שטרות are treated as paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone has among his papers a note saying 'The שטר of יוסף בן שמעון is paid,' then the שטרות of both of them are paid.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with the same two יוסף בן שמעון's. Here it rules on a note found among the lender's papers saying that one of them paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The note does not say which יוסף בן שמעון paid. We cannot tell which debt is still owed, so the lender cannot collect from either one, and both שטרות count as paid.
steps.whatToRemember: When a document cannot tell two people with the same name apart, the person holding the money keeps it. So the lender cannot collect from either man.

phrases.english: If it was found by someone among his documents:
phrases.notes: This is a lender who holds שטרות against both men named יוסף בן שמעון.

phrases.english: "The שטר of Yosef ben Shimon is paid" –
the שטרות of both of them are paid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the case of the two יוסף בן שמעון's from Step 12, now with a note saying one שטר was paid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A note saying 'יוסף בן שמעון's שטר is paid' makes both men's שטרות count as paid, since we cannot tell which one it means.

steps.title: How two people with the same name should write their documents
steps.stepSummary: The משנה gives the solution for two men with the same name in one city: add the grandfather's name, then a description, then 'כהן'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What should they do? They should write three generations of names. If even the three generations are the same, they should write a description. If even the descriptions are the same, they should write 'כהן'.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes the case of the two men named יוסף בן שמעון by telling them how to write their names so no one can confuse their שטרות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 12 and 13 showed the problem: when two men share a name, their שטרות and receipts get mixed up. Here the משנה gives a ladder of fixes. If one step still leaves them identical, you go to the next one: grandfather's name, then a description, then the title כהן.

keyTerms.meaning: they should 'triple' the name: write the person, his father, and his grandfather
already 'tripled', meaning even the grandfathers have the same name
an identifying sign or description that tells the two apart
a priest; writing this title separates a כהן from a non-כהן with the same name

steps.whatToRemember: The fix for identical names is a ladder: grandfather's name, then a description, then 'כהן'. Each step is only needed if the one before still leaves the two men identical.

phrases.english: What should they do? They should triple their names,
phrases.notes: 'Triple' means writing three generations, like 'יוסף son of שמעון son of so-and-so.'

phrases.english: and if they were tripled as well, they should write a sign,
phrases.notes: So even the grandfathers share a name. Then they add a description that tells the two apart.

phrases.english: and if they had the same signs as well, they should write 'כהן'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the practical solution to the confusion described in Steps 12 and 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two people with the same name should add three generations of names, then a description, then 'כהן', as each level is needed.

steps.title: A note with no lender's name comes before רב הונא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins with a story: a שטר came to רב הונא's בית דין that says 'I borrowed a מנה from you' but does not name the lender.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a certain שטר that came to the בית דין of רב הונא. Written in it was: 'I, so-and-so son of so-and-so, borrowed a מנה from you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new case. It describes a strange שטר, and the next lines will discuss what to do with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The שטר names the borrower but says only 'from you' for the lender. That leaves a big question open: who is allowed to collect with it? This links to the משנה's concern about unclear names in documents.

keyTerms.meaning: a document; here a loan document (שטר חוב)
so-and-so son of so-and-so; standing in for the borrower's real name
a sum of one hundred זוז

phrases.english: GEMARA: There was a certain document that came out
to the court of רב הונא,
in which it was written:
'I, so-and-so son of so-and-so,
borrowed a מנה from you.'
phrases.notes: Notice that it says 'from you' and never gives the lender's name. That missing name is the whole problem.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא שְׁטָרָא דִּנְפַק לְבֵי דִינָא דְּרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא on the new משנה with a story about a שטר whose lender is not named.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Case setup: a שטר names the borrower but leaves the lender unnamed ('from you').
